title: SpiderCSS: Scalable Fault-Tolerant CSS State Preparation
authors: Boldizsár Poór, Andrey Boris Khesin, Sarah Meng Li, Benjamin Rodatz, John van de Wetering, Richie Yeung
abstract: Fault-tolerant preparation of logical states is a critical primitive for the realization of large-scale fault-tolerant quantum computing. This paper introduces SpiderCSS, a scalable compilation pipeline that generates highly-optimized, fault-tolerant state preparation circuits for arbitrary Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) codes. Starting from an idealized specification of a CSS state, we use the ZX-calculus and fault-equivalent rewrites to construct a diagram that prepares the given state while preserving the fault tolerance of the initial ideal ZX-diagram. From this diagram, SpiderCSS constructs a fault-tolerant CSS-state preparation circuit using a modular construction that is CNOT-minimal both within each component and also in the way these components are connected together. By only using fault-equivalent rewrites, the final circuit is provably fault-tolerant without needing expensive verification. Monte Carlo simulations across a variety of CSS codes up to distance 15 show that SpiderCSS scales efficiently and constructs circuits with substantially reduced depth and qubit footprint compared to existing scalable and heuristic methods, while simultaneously achieving an average decrease of 33.7% in logical error rate and an increase of 9.5% in acceptance rate.
summary: This paper introduces SpiderCSS, a novel, scalable compilation pipeline for generating fault-tolerant circuits to prepare logical states in CSS quantum codes. By leveraging the ZX-calculus and fault-equivalent rewrites, it constructs highly optimized circuits that significantly reduce resource overhead compared to previous state-of-the-art methods. This advancement is crucial for realizing large-scale, reliable quantum computation.
main_problem: The paper addresses the critical need for a scalable and provably fault-tolerant method to prepare logical quantum states encoded within Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) codes.
main_result: The proposed SpiderCSS pipeline significantly outperforms existing methods by achieving substantial reductions in circuit depth and logical error rates while maintaining polynomial scaling with code size.
method: It utilizes the ZX-calculus and fault-equivalent rewrites to transform an idealized state specification into a highly optimized, fault-tolerant circuit construction.
model_or_system: The focus is on fault-tolerant quantum computation using CSS stabilizer codes. The analysis is formalized using the ZX-calculus, which maps quantum circuits to graph structures (ZX-diagrams).
key_observables: Logical error rate, acceptance rate, CNOT count, circuit depth, and qubit footprint.
important_parameters: Code distance (up to 15), Pauli noise model, and the efficiency of the compilation pipeline.
main_assumptions: The method relies on the stabilizer formalism and assumes that fault tolerance can be maintained by using fault-equivalent rewrites, simplifying the verification process.
figures_summary: Figure 1 compares SpiderCSS and Flag at Origin performance across various metrics (error rate, acceptance rate, depth, qubit count); Figure 2 illustrates the ZX-calculus translation between circuits and diagrams.
paper_structure: The paper builds from foundational definitions of fault tolerance and the ZX-calculus for CSS states, details the novel SpiderCSS compilation pipeline, and concludes with quantitative comparisons against state-of-the-art methods.
why_interesting: While focused on abstract quantum computation, the rigorous resource optimization techniques (minimizing CNOTs, depth) are highly relevant to designing physical quantum hardware implementations, such as those using trapped ions or superconducting qubits.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: Percentage improvements of SpiderCSS over Flag at Origin (FaO) across the benchmarked CSS states. Each point represents a CSS state, and the cross at the origin is the FaO baseline. Positive values mean SpiderCSS outperforms FaO (lower logical error rate, depth or qubit count; higher acceptance rate), so points in the shaded top-right quadrant improve on both metrics. Stars mark the mean improvements, with their values indicated on the axes.

FIG. 2: ZX overview. (a) Translation between quantum circuits and ZX-diagrams. The k parameter in the representation of Z- and X-measurements corresponds to the measurement outcome. Note that a Z-spider is used to represent an X-type measurement and state preparation, and vice versa for an X-spider. (b) A selection of ZX-rewrites. k, k1, k2 ∈{0, 1}.
FIG. 3: The rewrites together with their colour duals are fault-equivalent [17].

FIG. 4: Circuit extraction from a fault-tolerant Z-spider expansion. (a) A graph with eight marked output positions. (b) Its expanded graph with a spanning tree rooted at vertex 0. (c) The trivalent Z-graph obtained by attaching an output leg to each marked vertex. (d) The same Z-graph arranged for extraction. (e) The extracted CAT-state preparation circuit, with three verification ancillas. The mark q (vertex 6, teal) becomes output qubit q, while the non-tree edge ef = (2, 7) (orange) is implemented by the two CNOTs involving ancilla f. Numbers identify corresponding vertices and output ports, not spider phases. All three measurement outcomes are post-selected to 0.

FIG. 5: Transformation steps towards an extractable ZX-diagram for fault-tolerant state preparation. Step 1.1 brings the diagram into a row-reduced normal form, then, Step 1.2 unidealizes the internal edges, and Step 1.3 unfuses the spiders along safe hook errors (Step 1.3.1) and using SpiderCat [16] (Step 1.3.2).
